creator: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan (Facebook AI Research)
description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia (specifically Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage) and professionally translated into 101 languages. The dataset supports many-to-many multilingual evaluation (10,100 language pairs), document-level translation, and multimodal translation, with all translations produced by professional translators through a carefully controlled quality assurance process.

name: FLORES-101
rai:annotatorDemographics: Sentence selection was performed by 10 annotators in the lab: 6 male and 4 female, with different roles (researchers including scientists and engineers, and program/project managers), originally from different regions (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, and North America). Translation was performed by professional translators from Language Service Providers.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed using a Translation Quality Score (0-100 scale) per language. All 101 languages in FLORES-101 met the 90% quality threshold. About 50% of languages scored above 95%. 45 languages required re-translation, with an average of 1 re-translation and a maximum of 3. The largest error category across all languages was mistranslation.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Professional Language Service Providers (LSPs) — two translation LSPs and a separate quality assurance LSP
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Sentences were translated by professional Language Service Providers (LSPs). The workflow involved: (1) translation by an initial LSP including editing, (2) automatic quality checks (language identification, copy detection, length checks, fluency checks, and detection of copying from commercial translation engines), (3) human quality assurance by an independent LSP providing a Translation Quality Score on a 0-100 scale. Translations scoring below 90% were sent back for re-translation. Error categories examined included grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register.
rai:dataBiases: All source sentences are in English (from English Wikipedia), meaning non-English translations are produced by human translators and may exhibit translationese effects (overly literal or awkward translations). The authors acknowledge this but argue the effects are marginal for low-resource languages where MT systems make many severe mistakes. Additionally, automatic checks were implemented to prevent translators from copying commercial translation engine outputs, which would bias evaluation metrics.
rai:dataCollection: Sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia sources (Wikinews, Wikijunior, WikiVoyage). Articles were selected at random from each source, and 3-5 contiguous sentences were manually selected per article. Sentences were then professionally translated into 101 languages by Language Service Providers (LSPs) through a multi-stage workflow including translation, automatic quality checks, and human quality assurance by independent LSPs.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source sentences extracted from English Wikipedia, specifically from Wikinews (international news articles), Wikijunior (nonfiction books for children), and WikiVoyage (travel guide articles). Each sentence came with its Wikipedia URL, topic, and boolean flags indicating whether it contained hyperlinked entities or images.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Document analysis
rai:dataLimitations: All source sentences are from English Wikipedia, so non-English translations are produced by human translators and may exhibit translationese effects. The test set is not publicly released but is available via an evaluation server to prevent overfitting. Several languages considered for inclusion could not meet the 90% quality threshold after multiple rounds of re-translation and were excluded.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Sentences were balanced across three paragraph positions (beginning, middle, end of article) with roughly one third from each position. The 3001 sentences were divided into three splits: dev (997 sentences, 281 articles), devtest (1012 sentences, 281 articles), and test (992 sentences, 280 articles). Sentences were manually labeled by sub-topic into 10 categories.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Automatic quality checks were applied to translations: (i) language identification, (ii) checking whether the translation is a copy of the source sentence, (iii) checking whether the translation has significantly different length, (iv) checking translation fluency according to a language model, (v) checking whether the translation is a copy of output from publicly available translation engines. Translations with more than 10% of sentences violating the copy-detection criteria were sent for re-translation.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to foster progress in machine translation for low-resource languages, which are spoken by the majority of the world's population. By enabling evaluation of many-to-many translation including regionally-relevant language pairs (e.g., Spanish-Aymara, Vietnamese-Thai, Xhosa-Zulu), it supports development of non-English-centric translation systems that can benefit speakers of underrepresented languages.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of machine translation systems across 101 languages and up to 10,100 language pairs; many-to-many multilingual translation evaluation; document-level translation evaluation; multimodal translation evaluation; sentence and document classification; language identification; multilingual domain adaptation.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Language identification model; language model for fluency checking; commercial translation engines (used for copy-detection heuristic, comparing LSP translations against engine outputs using sentence-level SentencePiece BLEU); SentencePiece tokenizer trained on monolingual data from all FLORES-101 languages.

null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data in the collection process; languages that failed quality checks were excluded rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; the paper does not discuss filling in missing values.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No formal versioning or maintenance plan is described beyond a general hope to expand language coverage.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of translated Wikipedia text (news, travel, children's content) and does not contain personal or sensitive information.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The evidence quote discusses translation turnaround times, not the timeframe when data was collected. The extracted value is None, and the quote provides no information about collection start/end date
null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper describes a workflow where each sentence is translated once per language with possible re-translation rounds, but does not state a specific number of independent annotations per item in a way that maps cleanly to this field.

evidence.name: We present the FLORES-101 benchmark, consisting of 3001 sentences sampled from English Wikipedia and professionally translated in 101 languages.
evidence.description: We introduce the FLORES-101 evaluation benchmark, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and covering a variety of different topics and domains. These sentences have been translated in 101 languages by professional translators through a carefully controlled process.
evidence.url: the dev and devtest are publicly downloadable. https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/flores101/dataset/flores101_dataset.tar.gz

evidence.isLiveDataset: We hope to continue to expand the number of languages covered in FLORES-101 and make the test set available to various community efforts to improve translation systems in shared tasks such as those from the Workshop on Machine Translation.
evidence.rai:dataCollection: All source sentences were extracted from multiple Wikimedia sources, as this is a repository of text that is public and freely available under permissive licensing, and covers a broad range of topics. We collected a third of the sentences from Wikinews, which is a collection of international news articles, a third from Wikijunior, which is a collection of age-appropriate nonfiction books for children from birth to age 12, and a third from WikiVoyage which is a travel guide with a collection of articles about travel tips, food and destinations around the globe.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: All source sentences were extracted from multiple Wikimedia sources, as this is a repository of text that is public and freely available under permissive licensing, and covers a broad range of topics.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: For each sentence, we also extracted the Wikipedia URL, topic, and noted boolean flags to indicate whether the sentence contained entities linked to other Wikipedia pages and images.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: We assess translation quality through a Translation Quality Score, calculated per language on a 0 to 100 scale. The translation quality score is determined based on the number of identified errors by the evaluation LSPs. The following errors are examined: grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition or omission of information, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register. Each error is also associated with a severity level, between minor, major, and critical. Based on our pilot experiments, we set the acceptable translation quality score to 90%.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: we split our workﬂow into two parts: translation (which includes editing), performed by an initial LSP, and quality assurance (QA) performed by an independent LSP.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: The selection process was performed by 10 different annotators in our lab, 6 male and 4 female; with different roles in research: researchers (scientists and engineers) and program/project managers; originally coming from different regions of the world: East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America and North America.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All 101 languages in FLORES-101 meet our initial threshold of 90% quality based on human evaluation. Note that several languages were considered beyond our set of 101, but were unable to meet the bar after rounds of re-translation. Overall, about 50% of languages have fairly high quality (above 95%), with few near the 90% threshold boundary.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: For each language, all source sentences are sent to a certain translation LSPs. Once sentences are translated, the data is sent to different translators within the LSP for editing and then moves on to automated quality control steps.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We implemented several checks to ensure the first round of translations were of acceptable quality: (i) language identification, (ii) checking whether the translation is a copy of the source sentence; (iii) checking whether the translation has significantly different length, (iv) checking translation fluency according to a language model, (v) and checking whether the translation is a copy of the translation produced by publicly available translation engines.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: We implemented several checks to ensure the first round of translations were of acceptable quality: (i) language identification, (ii) checking whether the translation is a copy of the source sentence; (iii) checking whether the translation has significantly different length, (iv) checking translation fluency according to a language model, (v) and checking whether the translation is a copy of the translation produced by publicly available translation engines.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Beyond translation, FLORES-101 can be used to evaluate tasks such as sentence and document classification, language identification, and multilingual domain adaptation. We hope that the release of this dataset and our baseline M2M models will be useful for the community.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Yet, the majority of the world's population speak low-resource languages and would benefit from improvements in translation quality on their native languages. We hope that FLORES-101 can be used to develop non-English-centric models that directly translate between African languages.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: While translationese (or overly literal or awkward translations) has known idiosyncrasies (Zhang and Toral, 2019), we conjecture that these effects are rather marginal when evaluating models in low-resource languages, where current MT systems produce many severe mistakes.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: The test set will not be released, but will be available via a publicly available evaluation server, while the dev and devtest are publicly downloadable. The primary motivation for keeping the test set available only through an evaluation server is to guarantee equivalent assessment of models and reduce overfitting to the test set.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Avg # of Days to Translate 1 language 26, Avg # of Days to Re-Translate 35, Avg # of Days for 1 language 61, Shortest Turnaround (days) for 1 language 31, Longest Turnaround (days) for 1 language 89
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: To avoid bias coming from the document structure, we carefully selected one paragraph per document, from either the beginning, middle or end of the article. We balanced the location selection to be equally distributed across the whole corpus — roughly one third of paragraphs were sampled from the beginning of the article, one third from the middle, and so on.
